ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Thoracic Oncology Referral — Jesse Owens — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New patient visit: shared decision-making for lung cancer screening, same-day low-dose CT showing a suspicious left upper lobe nodule, and tobacco treatment

text.paragraph: Lung-RADS 4X nodule on a first low-dose screening CT in a 65-year-old man who smokes a pack a day (35 pack-years): a solid, spiculated 2.9 cm left upper lobe nodule with an enlarged 1.6 cm left hilar node. PET-CT and brain MRI are booked this week and EBUS staging after that. Please see him within two weeks to review the results with him and plan treatment if this is cancer. [S]

list.item: Is this lung cancer, and what is its stage? Which lymph node stations should be sampled, and is more staging needed?
Can it be removed, and what treatment do you recommend, in what order?
Which biomarkers must be back before treatment starts, and do any of them change the plan?
Is he fit for lung resection, and what preparation would help?
How should his smoking be treated alongside cancer care, and does stopping now still matter?
What monitoring should primary care share during and after treatment, and does he need palliative care?

text.paragraph: Asymptomatic apart from a long-standing morning smoker's cough; no weight loss, hemoptysis, bone pain or headache. Smokes a pack a day and has for about 35 years; two attempts to stop without medicine; no clinician had discussed lung cancer screening with him before. Screening chosen today after a shared decision-making discussion with a decision aid. CT also shows mild upper-lobe emphysema and moderate coronary calcification. Childhood pneumonia, nearly fatal; no other illness, operation or regular medicine; no known allergies. Weight 77.0 kg, blood pressure 134/82, oxygen saturation 95 percent; chest clear; no nodes or clubbing. Results today: hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, white cells 8.4, platelets 262; creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (eGFR 84); calcium 9.4 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase 84 U/L; albumin 4.2 g/dL; liver tests normal. Fully active (ECOG 0), walks 3 km most mornings; runs a small public relations business and speaks at schools and youth clubs. Lives with his wife near Phoenix. He wants plain answers quickly and the same care as anyone else [S]

list.item: He wants to know quickly and plainly whether the spot on the scan is cancer, and what can be done. [S]
He has smoked for 35 years, has failed to stop twice on his own, and worries that stopping now is pointless. [S]
No doctor had offered him a lung scan before; he wants the same care anyone else would get, without delay. [S]
He wants to keep speaking to young people and to keep walking every morning. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: James Cleveland (J.C.) Owens was born on September 12, 1913, in Oakville, Alabama, the youngest of the children of Henry and Mary Emma Owens, who were sharecroppers. The Ohio State University Libraries give ten children; contemporary newspaper accounts and his own account give nine. [D]

As a child in Alabama he worked in the fields with his family. At about 7 he had pneumonia and nearly died; a brother and a sister died during the same epidemic. He later described himself as a sickly, emaciated, poverty-stricken child, and said that his parents knew the family had to leave to survive. In the early 1920s the family moved north to Cleveland, following an older sister who had written home about jobs there. [D]

In Cleveland a teacher misheard his initials J.C. and called him Jesse, and the name stuck. Coached by Charles Riley from junior high school, he won the long jump, set a world record in the 220-yard dash and tied the world record in the 100-yard dash at the National Interscholastic Championship in 1933. [D]

At the Ohio State University, which he entered in 1933, he was barred from the men's dormitory because of his race, lived in a boarding house with other African American students, and could not eat in the restaurants along High Street. He worked as a freight elevator operator. At the Big Ten championships in May 1935 he set world records in the 220-yard dash, the 220-yard low hurdles and the long jump. [D]

At the 1936 Olympic Games in Berlin he won four gold medals, in the 100 meters, the 200 meters, the long jump and the 4 x 100-meter relay, and he was given a ticker-tape parade in New York on his return. [D]

The offers that followed the Games did not become steady work. He earned money racing against horses and local sprinters, and said that Black athletes were not allowed in any professional sport then. A dry-cleaning business he founded in 1938 went into debt, and he filed for personal bankruptcy in 1939. He owed taxes on his income after the Games, and decades later was in trouble with the Internal Revenue Service again for failing to file returns. He later worked through public relations firms, as a speaker, and with youth organizations. [D]

He met Minnie Ruth Solomon at Fairmount Junior High School in Cleveland in 1930; they married and had three daughters. In the early 1970s, with their children grown, they moved from Chicago, their home of more than 20 years, to the Phoenix area of Arizona. Ruth Owens died in 2001. [D]

The Ohio State University awarded him an honorary doctorate of athletic arts, and in 1976 he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom. He served on the board of directors of the U.S. Olympic Committee from 1973. [D]

He smoked cigarettes for decades: at his death newspapers described him as a pack-a-day smoker for the past 35 years, and his doctors said he had smoked about a pack a day. The Ohio State University Libraries call him a lifetime smoker. [D]

list.item: Solid, spiculated 2.9 cm nodule in the left upper lobe with an enlarged (1.6 cm) left hilar lymph node on today's low-dose screening CT, Lung-RADS 4X (very suspicious); no symptoms of lung cancer. PET-CT, tissue diagnosis and thoracic oncology review booked: active, confirmed [S]

Nicotine dependence, cigarettes: a pack a day for 35 years (35 pack-years); smokes his first cigarette within 30 minutes of waking; two attempts to stop, each lasting a few weeks without medicine: active, confirmed [S]

Work-up of the Lung-RADS 4X nodule without delay: FDG PET-CT and brain MRI with contrast this week, then endobronchial ultrasound with systematic sampling of mediastinal and hilar nodes (at least stations 4R, 4L and 7, and any PET-avid node), with enough tissue for PD-L1 and comprehensive next-generation sequencing (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS, MET exon 14, RET, NTRK, HER2) and plasma testing in parallel; nurse navigator to track each date. Guideline: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (2026); US Preventive Services Task Force. Screening for Lung Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement. JAMA 2021;325(10):962-970 (PMID 33687470) (2021); Mazzone PJ, et al. Screening for Lung Cancer: CHEST Guideline and Expert Panel Report. Chest 2021;160(5):e427-e494 (PMID 34270968) (2021); Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) v2022 (2022); Silvestri GA, et al. Methods for staging non-small cell lung cancer: Diagnosis and management of lung cancer, 3rd ed: ACCP evidence-based clinical practice guidelines. Chest 2013;143(5 Suppl):e211S-e250S (PMID 23649440) (2013) [S]

Tobacco treatment at every visit: brief advice, varenicline offered with a quit date, the Arizona quitline and counseling; stopping smoking improves outcomes even after a lung cancer diagnosis. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, lung cancer monograph (2026); Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons: Interventions (2021) [S]

Equity safeguards: a nurse navigator, written results and next steps at each visit, transport and cost help offered, and time from scan to treatment tracked against the goal. Guideline: Aldrich MC, et al. Evaluation of USPSTF Lung Cancer Screening Guidelines Among African American Adult Smokers. JAMA Oncol 2019;5(9):1318-1324 (PMID 31246249) (2019); Bach PB, et al. Racial differences in the treatment of early-stage lung cancer. N Engl J Med 1999;341(16):1198-1205 (PMID 10519898) (1999) [S]

Distress and depression screening at each visit, plain information he can share, and advance care planning when he is ready. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, lung cancer monograph (2026) [S]
Referral to thoracic oncology, Ngozi Halvorsen-Pierce, MD, ordered 1979-05-11 [S]
